what_it_does: Resistive RAM (RRAM) is a type of memory chip that stores values by changing the electrical resistance of a material — it can also do math (multiply-accumulate operations) right where data sits, skipping costly transfers to a separate processor. The problem is that writing precise resistance values is unreliable: the same programming pulse produces slightly different resistances each time, making the stored AI model weights imprecise. Standard ways to protect a deployed AI model (encrypting its weights) also do not translate well to this physics. Guarder addresses both problems together: on the hardware side, a 3T2R cell (a circuit using three transistors and two resistive elements) stabilizes computation and encodes an encryption key directly in the resistance values; on the software side, the AI model is trained with a contrastive loss so it gives correct answers only when the decryption key in the hardware matches — unauthorized chips that lack the right key produce degraded, useless outputs.
